cover.topic: Community life, nature, geography and history

sections.title: Booking a community hall for a party
sections.context: You will hear a man phoning a community hall in Leeds to book a room for a family party.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Good morning, Northgate Community Hall, Rachel speaking. How can I help?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Oh, hello. I'd like to hire a room for a party, please. Do you have anything free in March?

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: We might have. Let me get the booking form up on my screen. Right, I'm ready. Could I take your name first?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Yes, it's Callum Fairbairn.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Sorry, could you spell the surname for me?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Of course. Fairbairn is F-A-I-R-B-A-I-R-N.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: F-A-I-R-B-A-I-R-N. Lovely, thank you, Mr Fairbairn. And is there a contact number?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: It's my mobile. 07700 900 413.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: 07700 900 413. Great. And what sort of event are we talking about? A birthday?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Well, that's what most people guess! No, actually it's a retirement party. My father finishes work after thirty-eight years at the council, and the family wants to surprise him.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Oh, how nice. A retirement party, then. And which date did you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: I was hoping for Saturday 12 March.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Hmm, let me check the diary. Ah, I'm afraid the twelfth is gone. We have a wedding reception in that day. But the following Saturday is free, and that would be 19 March.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: That's actually better, because my aunt is travelling down from Glasgow that weekend. Yes, let's say 19 March.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Perfect. I'll pencil that in. How many guests do you expect?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: I think about 80. Well, let me think. Eighty was the number on my first list, but several cousins can't come now. So it's more like 60, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Sixty is fine. That matters because we have three rooms. The Oak Room holds thirty, the main hall holds a hundred and fifty, and in between there's the Willow Room, which takes up to seventy. For your numbers, I'd suggest the Willow Room. It has its own little kitchen as well.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: That sounds ideal. Does it have a stage? My brother wants to make a speech.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: There's a small raised platform at one end, so he can stand up there. Now, you'd probably want the room from six until eleven in the evening. The price for that is £110.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Right. That's a bit more than I expected.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Oh, hold on, I'm so sorry. I was reading the old price list. From January the council has helped with the costs, so it's £95 for the evening.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Oh, that's much better. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: We also ask for a deposit to hold the date. That's £40, and you can pay it by card over the phone. The rest is paid on the night, before you leave.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: That's fine. I can do that today.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Wonderful. Do you need any equipment? We have tables and chairs, of course, and a projector, and we can provide a microphone too.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: A microphone would be useful for the speeches. We'll bring our own music on a speaker, and some photographs on a laptop, so I don't think we need the projector.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: No problem. Just let me note that down.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Is there parking? Quite a few of the guests are coming by car.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: There's a small car park behind the hall with room for about twenty cars, and there's plenty of street parking on Saturday evenings. The hall also has a ramp at the side door, so it's easy for anyone who has trouble with steps.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: That's good to know, because my grandmother uses a wheelchair. And can we bring in our own food?

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Yes, outside caterers are fine. You just have to clear everything away and leave the kitchen clean by half past eleven. The toilets are on the ground floor too, so your grandmother will be fine.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Last of all, where shall we send the confirmation and the invoice?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: It's 28 Beckett Road, Headingley, Leeds. The postcode is a little tricky. It's L-S-6, then 2-Q-T. So that's LS6 2QT.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: LS6 2QT. Thank you. You'll get an email and a letter within three days. If you want to come and see the room first, you're welcome any weekday between ten and four.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Oh, I'd love that. I might pop in on Thursday, if that's all right.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Of course. Just ask for me at the front desk. Thank you for calling, Mr Fairbairn, and enjoy planning the party.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Thanks very much, Rachel. Goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Goodbye.

sections.title: Volunteer briefing at a coastal nature reserve
sections.context: You will hear the warden of a nature reserve on the Northumberland coast briefing new volunteers.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Skerry Point Nature Reserve. My name is Fiona, and I'm the warden here. Thank you all for giving up your Saturday. Before we go out, I'd like to explain how a volunteer day works, and then tell you where we need help.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: First, timing. Shifts used to start at half past seven, but the early start put quite a few people off, so from this season we begin at 8 o'clock. We finish at about three, with a lunch break in the middle. Lunch is provided by the Friends of Skerry Point, so you don't need to bring sandwiches, but do bring a bottle of water.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Next, parking. Please don't use the car park beside the visitor centre. It's reserved for visitors and for people with limited mobility. The track down to the old lighthouse is closed at the moment, so the best place is the village car park, which is only a five minute walk. There's no charge for volunteers if you show the badge I'll give you today.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Now, what to wear. We'll lend you a bright jacket, and gloves if you need them. What we can't lend you is footwear. The ground is very wet at this time of year, so please wear waterproof boots. Ordinary trainers won't last ten minutes on the marsh, I promise you.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: A word about the paths. The east path along the cliff is closed until the end of August. Arctic terns have nested on the grass beside it, and they're very protective of their eggs. Some of you may have been told the path is closed because of erosion. That was true last year, but this year it's the birds. Please keep to the signed routes and don't go looking for them.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: So what will you actually be doing today? Our original plan was to count seals on the beach. But the seals haven't come ashore yet, so that will wait until next month. We'd also thought about repairing the fencing, but a team finished that last week. What we really need is help with sea buckthorn. It's a thorny shrub that spreads across the dunes and crowds out the smaller native plants, so we'll be clearing it by hand.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Let me now take you round the reserve in your minds. We'll start at the bird hide, which looks over the estuary. A small group will be based there. Their job is to record the numbers of each species they see, and they'll fill in the sheet every half hour. You don't need to be an expert. There are pictures of all the common birds on the wall.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: From the hide, a boardwalk runs across the soft ground to the beach. It was built twenty years ago, and several of the planks have gone soft and slippery. Two volunteers will replace the worst ones. Carpenters are very welcome, but I'll show anyone how to do it.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Halfway along the boardwalk you'll see the pond. In winter we cut back the reeds there, but that's finished, so today the job is something different. We take water samples to check how clean the water is, and a student from the university will show you how to use the testing kit. It's easier than it sounds.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Then there are the dunes. That's where the sea buckthorn is, as I said. Gloves are essential, please, because the thorns are sharp. Whoever works there will probably end up the muddiest, but also the proudest.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Finally, the visitor centre. We have a lot of families on Saturdays, so we always need one or two people at the door to hand out leaflets and answer questions. If you're happier talking to people than pulling up bushes, that's the place for you. We don't ask anyone to paint signs today, because the new ones haven't arrived yet.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Safety next. Always work in pairs. Radios are in the box by the door, and the emergency number is written on the back of your badge. If the tide comes in over the causeway, don't try to cross. Wait, and call me. The tide tables are pinned up in the hut, and I'll walk through them with you now.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: There will be tea and biscuits at the hut at eleven, and at the end of the day we'll look at what you've found. Last month, a volunteer found a rare moth on the dunes, and that made the local paper. So keep your eyes open. Right, does anyone have any questions before we set off?

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Good. Then let's choose pairs, collect your jackets from the hut, and head out. Mind the steps. They are slippery.

groups.title: Questions 11-15
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

sections.title: Planning a river fieldwork report
sections.context: You will hear two geography students discussing their river erosion fieldwork report with their tutor.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Come in, both of you. Sit down. So, you wanted to talk about the river project. How did the fieldwork go?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Mostly well, Dr Patel, though we had a few problems. We studied bank erosion on the River Wharfe, just outside Otley.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Hannah wanted to change the site halfway through, which caused some trouble.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: That's not quite fair, Liam. The first site was upstream by the weir, and when we got there the bank had been covered in concrete. There was nothing natural to measure, so we moved to a bend two kilometres further down.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Yes, that's true. I was cross at the time, but looking back it was the right decision. The new site had a proper outer bend, with a steep eroding bank.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Good. Outer bends are exactly where you'd expect the fastest erosion. How did you measure it?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: We used erosion pins. We pushed thirty of them into the bank in three rows, and then measured how much of each pin was showing.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Thirty seemed like plenty to me. But I've been thinking, and maybe it wasn't enough. We only had one visit, so we can't show change over time.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Well, a single visit is a limitation, certainly. But thirty pins is a reasonable sample for a student project. I wouldn't worry about the number. I'd worry more about repeating the measurements. Could you go back in two weeks?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: We could, if the river doesn't flood. It's been raining a lot.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: That would be ideal, actually. A flood would give you fascinating data. But before you go back, remember the safety form. Did you complete a risk assessment the first time?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Yes, we did, and we wore life jackets near the water, though the bank was only knee deep at the edge.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: I felt a bit silly in mine, but Hannah insisted.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Quite right. Rivers rise very quickly, and the department will not let you work alone. Take a third person with you if you can, and tell someone where you are going.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: We'll ask Priya from our group. She wanted to come anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Good. Now, what about the equipment? Did anything go wrong?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Quite a lot, really. The GPS unit ran out of battery after an hour, so we only have grid references for the first ten pins.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: And I thought the tape measure was too short for the wide section, but in the end we managed with two people. The bigger problem was the pins. Some of them had worked loose by the time we measured them. The soil was so soft that they moved.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd say that's more serious than the battery. We can't trust those readings.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: So the pins that moved are a problem for accuracy, while the GPS is only an inconvenience. You can mark the missing positions from your photographs. Did you take any?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Plenty. Although my phone fell into the water on the second day, so I lost half of them.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Luckily mine are fine. We have the whole bank covered.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Excellent. Let's talk about the missing readings. Would you leave them out, or try to estimate them?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I'd estimate them from the neighbouring pins.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: I disagree. I think it's better to leave them out and say so honestly. If we make numbers up, the results lose their value.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Liam is right. Never invent data. Leave the gaps, and explain them in your discussion. Now, let's look at your draft. I read it last night. Your introduction first. It's clear, but at the moment it's much too long. Cut it by about a third.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: We included lots of background reading.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: I can see that. In fact your use of the literature is very strong, which is a real credit to you, but you must be selective. The methods section is what I'd like to praise most. It's detailed enough that someone could repeat your work.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: That's good to hear. I wrote most of it.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: The results are where you need to improve. The tables are fine, but your diagrams are hard to read. The labels are tiny. A clear map showing your pins would help too.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: We do have a map, but it's in the appendix.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Then move it into the results. And finally the discussion. You must say what the weaknesses are. Be honest about the single visit and the loose pins. Markers always reward that kind of honesty.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: So the missing readings go there as well.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Exactly. Your conclusion should also answer your original question directly. What was it again?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Whether erosion is faster on the outer bank.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: And on our evidence it looks as if it is, though only two rows show clear change.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Then say exactly that, and no more. Don't claim more than the evidence shows. One more thing about timing. Many students leave the writing too late. How are you planning to share out the work?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Liam will write up the results, and I'll do the discussion and the introduction.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Actually, I'd prefer to try the discussion myself, if Hannah doesn't mind. I did the methods, and I'd like to practise something more analytical.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: That's fine with me. I'll take the introduction and check all the references.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: A sensible plan, as long as one of you reads the whole thing at the end so that it sounds like a single voice. The deadline is Friday week, so you have time. Come back on Wednesday if you'd like me to read it again.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Thank you very much.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Yes, thanks. That was really helpful.

sections.title: The history of the Penny Post
sections.context: You will hear a history lecturer talking about how the postal system in Britain changed in the nineteenth century.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about one of the quiet revolutions of the nineteenth century, the reform of the British postal system. We tend to take the post for granted. But for most of history, sending a letter was expensive, slow and surprisingly unfair. Let me begin by explaining how things worked before 1840.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In those days, the person who paid for the letter was not the person who wrote it. The charge was paid by the recipient. You can imagine what that meant. If a letter arrived, you had to pay before you were even allowed to read it. And if you didn't want the news, or couldn't afford it, you could simply refuse the letter. Some clever people used this to their advantage. They would write a secret message on the outside of the envelope, and then the receiver would read it and send the letter back without paying a penny.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The price itself was complicated. It depended mainly on how far the letter travelled, but also on the number of sheets of paper inside. A letter of one sheet cost less than a letter of two sheets, so people wrote on both sides, crossed their lines, and used the thinnest paper they could find. An envelope counted as an extra sheet, so most people didn't use one. They folded the letter and sealed it with wax.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The reformer who changed all this was Rowland Hill. Hill was a teacher by profession. He had run a school near Birmingham, and he understood both mathematics and the daily life of ordinary families. Later he moved to the Post Office, and what he found there astonished him. The real cost of carrying a letter, he argued, was tiny. Most of the expense lay in the handling and in collecting the money at the door.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In 1837 he published a pamphlet called Post Office Reform. It made a simple proposal: charge a single low price, one penny, for any letter up to half an ounce, anywhere in the country, and make the sender pay in advance. Many officials thought the idea was ridiculous. They believed the Post Office would lose a fortune. But the public was strongly in favour, and after a long campaign Parliament agreed.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Pre-payment needed something to prove that the postage had been paid. That is why the first adhesive postage stamp was invented. The Penny Black went on sale in 1840. Stamps were printed on large sheets, and each sheet held 240 stamps. That number was chosen deliberately, because there were 240 pennies in one pound, so a whole sheet cost exactly one pound. There were no perforations at that time. Post office clerks and customers had to separate the stamps with scissors, and if you look at old stamps today, you will often see uneven edges.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The design was simple and elegant. It showed a small portrait of the young Queen Victoria, who was only eighteen when she came to the throne. The same portrait was used on British stamps for the next sixty years, even though the queen herself grew old. Hill wanted a picture that was hard to copy, and a royal portrait was one of the best ways to make that possible.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Did it succeed? Spectacularly. In 1839, the last year of the old system, about 76 million letters were sent in Britain. A year later, in 1840, the figure had more than doubled to 169 million. In the following decade it doubled again. Letters became part of everyday life. People who had never written to a distant relative now sent birthday wishes, news of illness, and invitations. Love letters and business letters flowed together through the same sacks.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Of course, there were a few problems. The Penny Black was cancelled with red ink, but red ink can be hard to see on a black stamp, and people soon found they could wash it off and use the stamp again. So in 1841 the colour was changed. The new stamp was the Penny Red, with the cancellation printed in black. It stayed in use for nearly forty years.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Another improvement came with perforations. In 1854 the first perforated stamps appeared, with tiny holes between each stamp so that they could be torn apart easily. It sounds a small thing, but it saved countless hours for clerks and shopkeepers, and the idea quickly spread to other countries.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: One last development I want to mention is the way people posted their letters. In the early days, you had to take your letter to a receiving office, and these were few and far between. The solution was the roadside pillar box. The first ones in Britain appeared in the 1850s, and a Post Office official who helped introduce them was the novelist Anthony Trollope. He saw them as a practical way of bringing the service to people's doors.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So, to sum up, the Penny Post began as a simple idea from a teacher, but it changed how a whole society communicated. Next week we'll look at the telegraph, and ask whether the same kind of change happened again.
